narrative:
The model determined that you have an 83.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants to admit students likely to succeed, this prediction led to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the model toward predicting failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of roughly the sixth and fifth deciles among students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the bar exam.

Your family income bracket was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in the opposite direction. Being from an upper-middle-income family slightly increased the model’s confidence that you might pass, yet this positive influence was not nearly strong enough to overcome the academic concerns.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently low class standing as clear evidence that the risk of bar failure was too high for admission. 

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, or consider retaking key courses, seeking additional bar-prep support, or applying to schools with different risk thresholds. Improving your class rank in future semesters could meaningfully change how a similar model evaluates you. (218 words)
